1:
The change of place is noticed by everyone and explained differently. Bede harmonises it with the first Gospel, where this teaching falls on the same day as the sermon before it, and reads the move allegorically: leaving the house and the synagogue, he taught at the sea because he was coming to gather the Gentiles by the Apostles. Henry keeps it practical. The previous chapter opened with Christ entering the synagogue and this one with his teaching by the water, the method changed so that all might be reached: the synagogue had chief seats for the nicer sort who would hear a sermon nowhere else, and the shore was for the poor. Robertson describes the sequence, that he sat first on the beach until the crowd pushed him into a boat, and says one can see the people pressing him into the sea. Gill fixes the day, the same as the dispute in the house at Capernaum.

Chrysostom asks why the boat at all and answers twice. The first is practical, that he might leave nobody behind him but have every hearer before his face, and that a parable rouses the mind by putting objects before the sight. The second is not: he did not go out in space, being present in all space and filling it, but in the form by which the clothing of flesh brings him nearer, since we could not go to him, our sins having blocked the path.

Lightfoot supplies two notes from the rabbis that nobody else has. The first is idiom: he began to teach means simply that he taught, a turn very usual to the nation, as when a rabbi is said to have begun to be tedious in his prayer, meaning that he was tedious, or the ox to have begun to low, meaning that it lowed. The second explains how seed could fall in such different places at once, since sowing was done sometimes by hand and sometimes by loading the seed into a cart full of holes and driving the oxen over the ploughed ground, so that the rabbis distinguish seed falling from the hand and seed falling from the oxen. On the stony ground he adds that rock is not barrenness, the land about Hebron being rocky and yet reckoned to exceed the most fruitful part of Egypt sevenfold; what the parable supposes is a thin turf, not a poor one.

Wesley defines the term before the parable is pressed: it covers not only a simile and sometimes a proverb, but any instructive speech in which spiritual things are explained by natural ones; and he supposes the opening word was spoken loudly, to quiet the noise of the crowd.

Robertson collects what belongs to this evangelist alone. The verb for choking is a compound meaning squeezed together, where the first Gospel has choked off; the clause that the seed yielded no fruit is in this Gospel only; and so are the words about the good seed growing up and increasing, which make the yielding continuous, so that it kept on bearing as it grew. Ellicott finds independence in the numbers: the parable is almost word for word what the other evangelist has, except that the scale of the harvest ascends here where it descends there.

Clarke keeps to the text. The phrase about the fowls of the air should lose its last two words, he argues, on the authority of nine uncial manuscripts and almost all the versions, the words having probably come in from the third Gospel; and at the close he reports an addition found in one old codex, that whoever understands should understand. Augustine looks past the sowing to the hearers who would not understand, and refuses to make their failure merely punitive: they deserved it, and yet even this was done in mercy, that they might know their sins and, turning, earn pardon.
10:
Who was listening in private is a small point that three of them think worth making. Clarke observes that no other evangelist hints at anyone besides the twelve being there, whereas this one shows several others present who, though not styled disciples, were attending seriously to the public and private teaching alike. Ellicott makes the same comparison shorter, that the first Gospel says simply the disciples while here the presence of others beyond the Twelve is directly asserted. Robertson adds that the phrase about his being alone belongs to this Gospel only and reads like Peter remembering, and then supplies a motive nobody else offers: they did not want the crowd to see that they had not understood. Gill notes only that the multitude had been dismissed, and that some versions make the whole company rather than Christ the subject of the being alone.

The phrase about those without is explained from Jewish usage. Lightfoot reports that in that speech those without were the Gentiles, the expression coming from the habit of calling every country besides their own the land without, and he gives a rabbinic instance of the distinction being pressed, a tree growing half inside the land and half outside and the difficulty this made for tithing its fruit. Wesley gives the same origin and then extends the term as he thinks Christ does, to all obstinate unbelievers, who shall abide in outer darkness. Ellicott points out that the form of the phrase is peculiar to this evangelist, the others having to them and to the rest.

On the word for mystery Robertson gathers the statistics, that it stands here alone in the Gospels while it is frequent in Daniel and occurs twenty-one times in Paul; and he presses a difference of construction, that the others write it plural and add the words to know, where this Gospel gives the thing itself, which covers more than growing knowledge, since the mystery may be possessed before it is understood. Clarke is interested in the same two words for the opposite reason, because several manuscripts omit them, and the omission alters the sense materially: without them the sentence reads that to you the mystery of the kingdom is given, but that to those without all these things are done in parables. He reports one editor leaving it doubtful and another judging the words probably to be deleted, and says he would incline to omit them himself were they not found in both parallel places.

The clause about seeing and not perceiving is the hard one, and four of them answer it without agreeing on method. Ellicott notes that the words of the prophet are given here not as a quotation and perhaps less accurately, with the beatitude on the hearers' eyes and ears left out, and admits that the form at first sight suggests that blindness was the purpose; the real meaning, he holds, is that this was to be the result of a wilful blindness in those who rejected him. Robertson refuses that escape on grammatical grounds, since there is no way to give the particle a causal sense, and accepts instead that what is expressed is a purpose of condemnation, aimed at exactly the wilful blindness the Pharisees had shown in their accusation. Calvin reaches the same place by an image rather than a grammar: doctrine is not in its own nature the cause of blindness but only by accident, as a man of weak sight is dazzled by coming into the sun, where the defect belongs to the eyes and not to the sun; so when the word hardens the reprobate it does so through their own depravity. Wesley compresses all of it into one sentence, that they would not see, and now could not, God having given them up to the blindness they had chosen.
13:
The rebuke that opens the interpretation is found in this Gospel alone, as Clarke points out, and the commentators take it as aimed at the disciples' future work rather than at their present slowness only. Barnes reads the two halves against each other, that this parable is plain and obvious while others are difficult and obscure, and infers that men who were themselves to be teachers needed the whole system of religion much more than the mass of the people did. Clarke says the same of the method, that they ought to become perfect masters of this way of teaching in order to use it on others. Wesley calls the parable the foundation of all that were to follow. Robertson hears surprise in the question, since these were men already initiated into the secret of the kingdom, and draws the consequence plainly: an incapacity to take in this one puts every other parable in doubt. Ellicott turns the question forward instead of back, finding in it the expectation of an ever-growing insight, not into the spoken parables only but into those of nature and of life; and he puts the difficulty that raises, how such insight was to be imparted to scholars so slow at this early stage, and answers that the interpretation which follows is the first lesson in it.

What the seed is Robertson notes is stated here more clearly and simply than in either of the parallel accounts. Gill takes the point and applies it through the four soils, the casual hearer who stops a while by the way, the hearer whose heart has never been broken and who has a speculative knowledge and a flashy affection but no root, the hearer eaten up with worldly care, and the hearer made good by grace, in whom the word finds a heart already disposed to receive it.

Robertson collects the small differences that mark this account. The clause explaining where the word is sown is peculiar to it; the adversary is named here where the other two Gospels have the evil one and the devil; and the seed is described as sown within the hearers rather than merely among them.

Clarke works from the Latin copies and finds the reading that interests him at the way side, where four of them have it that those sown there are the men who receive the word negligently. He does not leave that as a textual note but turns it on the reader directly, observing that there are thousands of this stamp in the Christian world and asking whether the reader is one of them. At the thorns he reports the same copies varying again, some giving the errors of the world and some its delights, and one saying that such men are completely alienated by its pleasures; and having listed them he adds only that all of these choke the word.

The last of the three hindrances is handled carefully by two of them. Robertson describes the longings meant as the passions and desires of the world of sense drowning the world of spirit, and then enters a qualification the passage might otherwise seem to exclude, that the word itself is not an evil one and can be used of yearning for what is high and holy. Wesley presses the same clause harder and calls the truth in it deep and important: the desire of anything, otherwise than as it leads to happiness in God, tends directly to barrenness of soul. He notices that these desires are said to enter in, which means they were not there before, and warns the man who has received and kept the word to see that no new desire enters, of a kind he may until then never have known.
21:
The candle is read as a statement about the parables by most of them, and allegorically by two. Chrysostom takes it as the reason for the method: a parable is given not that it should stay hidden under a bed or a bushel but that it should be made plain to those who are worthy, the candle within us being our intellectual nature, which shines clearly or dimly in proportion to what we bring to it. Barnes says the same without the allegory: a lamp is not lit to be put under a measure where it can give no light, so the preaching in parables is meant to throw light on the truth, and those who understand are to pass it on. Wesley adds that whatever is concealed from them now is concealed only that it may be manifested the more effectually afterwards.

Bede works the furniture of the room into a figure. The bushel is the measured span of a life under providence and the bed is the body, where the soul dwells and rests a while, so a man covers his candle with either when he hides the word under the love of this transitory life; he sets his light on a candlestick when he employs the body itself in the ministry of the word. Henry turns the image into an obligation: God expects a grateful return of his gifts to us and a useful improvement of his gifts in us.

Two notes stand apart from the exposition. Ellicott observes what this evangelist has done with his materials, leaving out the other parables that follow in the first Gospel and attaching to the Sower a set of proverbial sayings which there appear in another context, which he takes for evidence of a habit of repeating the same proverb under different aspects. Robertson records what he calls a curious instance of early corruption, the two oldest manuscripts both reading under the lampstand where the sense requires upon it.

On the saying that nothing is hidden the three differ in scope. Clarke makes it historical, that what had been secret about the salvation of the world, or pointed at only through types and sacrifices, is now uncovered by the gospel; the design of his preaching, he says elsewhere, was never to hide the truth but to make it more manifest. Robertson makes it purposive, the concealment being temporary and itself the means to a final manifestation, the men entrusted with the secret now being charged to proclaim it from the housetops afterwards.

The measure is the last figure and the most variously applied. Ellicott uses it to illustrate his own point about repetition, since in the Sermon on the Mount the same proverb states the law of retribution, pardon for those who pardon, while here it is transferred to another region and governs knowledge. Barnes and Wesley agree on the practice, that a man is dealt with according to the use he makes of his opportunities, further assistance following the improvement of what has been heard. Robertson sets the two forms side by side, what ye hear here and how ye hear in the third Gospel, and thinks both matter, since some things ought not to be heard at all, besmirching the mind of anyone who takes them in. Clarke reports that the clause promising more to those who hear is missing from several copies and variously written where present, and that one editor struck it out as a gloss. On the closing paradox Robertson suggests the verb may carry the sense of acquiring, so the man who does not go on acquiring loses even what he supposes himself to hold. Barnes and Gill make it a rule of diligence, the attentive hearer increasing in knowledge while the negligent forgets the little he had learned.
26:
This is the one parable peculiar to the second Gospel, and two of them make something of the fact. Ellicott observes that it escaped the eagerness of the other evangelists to gather up everything of this form, and reads it as running parallel to the Sower. Clarke draws a conclusion from its presence here, that a parable found in this Gospel and no other proves its writer was not abridging the first;

Whom the sower stands for is where they part. Calvin thinks the discourse aimed at the ministers of the word, to keep them from growing indifferent because the fruit of their labour does not appear at once, and holds out the husbandman for imitation, who sows in expectation of a harvest and does not torment himself in the interval. Wesley makes the seed the inward kingdom and the sower a preacher casting it into the heart, reading the sleeping and rising as meaning that he has it continually in his thoughts. Gill excludes two wrong senses of that sleep, neither natural sleep nor spiritual sloth, since neither belongs to a true minister. Gregory takes the man for any believer: he casts seed when he sets a good intention in his heart, sleeps when he rests in the hope attending a good work, and rises night and day because he advances through prosperity and adversity without knowing it, virtue once conceived going on increasing.

On the sower's ignorance they agree and press it differently. Barnes says the man lives in his usual way and exerts no influence over the growing grain, warning against the inference that no diligence is required, since the point is only that we cannot tell how grain grows. Clarke says flatly that how a plant grows is a mystery which the wisest philosopher cannot explain, and Robertson brings it up to date, that it still puzzles farmers and scientists; he notes too the word order, which throws the emphasis on the man's not knowing.

The phrase about the earth bringing forth of herself is handled four ways that do not conflict. Robertson renders it automatically and locates the secret of growth in the seed rather than in soil or weather or cultivation, which all help without supplying it; the word occurs only once more in the New Testament, of a city gate opening of its own accord. Clarke supports the same sense from a Latin poet who says some trees come of their own accord without the labour of man. Barnes cautions that the passage does not require us to credit the earth with a productive power of its own, only to deny that the power is man's, since God gives it. Ellicott draws the lesson rather than the mechanism: the spontaneity teaches patience, and it is not well in spiritual husbandry to be taking up the seeds to see whether they are growing. He extends this to history, where philosophers and statesmen ignored the new force and even the sowers were hardly conscious of the revolution they were making.

The sickle divides them at the last. Barnes suggests that as ripe grain is cut down, so the Christian is often taken as soon as he is fit for heaven, then checks himself, since every parable carries circumstances put in to fill out the story. Clarke refuses it outright: it has been supposed that a soul made completely holy is taken at once into the kingdom, but the parable certainly does not say so. Ellicott keeps both levels, the harvest being the end of the world and the sickle the coming of Christ to judge, or the harvest the end of each man's life and the sickle in another hand. Robertson notes with Clarke that the sickle stands by metonymy for the reapers, and Wesley reduces the whole to a sentence, that God cuts down and gathers the corn into his garner.
30:
The double question that opens the parable is noticed as a device. Ellicott renders it literally as asking by what parable the thing shall be set forth, observes that it stands in this Gospel and the third but not the first, and reads it as put so as to stretch the hearers' minds and make them welcome the answer. Robertson calls it fine tact, drawing interest by asking rather than announcing. Barnes and Clarke both turn it into a lesson for preachers. Barnes finds in it the solicitude of a teacher adapting himself to his hearers and seeking the plainest and most striking illustrations, and adds that pulpit instruction, while dignified, should also be plain. Clarke is warmer, calling the carefulness amiable and instructive: the speaker looks for no fine turns of eloquence, nor comparisons that may surprise, but studies only to be understood.

Bede reports both readings of the sower, that many take him for the Saviour and others for a man sowing in his own heart. Chrysostom fixes on the disproportion the parable turns upon, that the wisdom spoken among the perfect expands further than any other saying, since there is nothing greater than this truth; and he notices the habit of the evangelist himself, who delights in brevity, and so adds a short remark about many such parables rather than reporting them.

Robertson handles the seed as a matter of language. The clause about its being sown belongs to this Gospel and is repeated; the claim that it is less than all seeds is hyperbole, but means plainly that a large plant grows from a very small one, which is the expansive power of the kingdom; and the birds are placed differently in the two accounts, under the shadow here and in the branches there, though the same verb is used in both, a word for tenting or camping down. Gill takes the kingdom to mean the Gospel, or the Gospel church state, or the grace of God in his people, and thinks it may include all three; the growth he traces in the history, where the preaching spread although a council charged the apostles to speak no more in that name.

The closing remark about hearing draws the most comment. Robertson points out that the clause is in this Gospel alone and marks a limit: parables were used largely now, but even they had a bound with these men, and the veiled form was the only feasible one at this stage. Barnes says the hearers were like children and had to be led cautiously and by degrees. Wesley states the principle and presses it on the reader, that the speaker adapted his matter to his hearers' capacity and spoke as plainly as he could without giving offence, a rule he says is never to be forgotten by those who instruct others. Clarke leaves exposition for text and reports that the word for many is missing from a number of manuscripts, one editor approving the omission and another leaving it doubtful; he takes it for an interpolation.

On the private exposition they are complementary. Barnes explains the restriction, that the parables covered the things of the kingdom while other subjects were spoken of plainly, prejudice being so strong and plain instruction so liable to offend that this method insinuated the truth by degrees. Robertson notes the tense, which makes the disclosing a habit rather than an occasion, and the emphasis on his own disciples as against the mass of the people. Ellicott adds an observation reaching outside the passage, that the verb here is the one behind the noun for interpretation in the second Epistle of Peter, one of the coincidences of phrasing connecting that letter with this Gospel. Clarke draws the inference, that outside hearers who never come into close fellowship with the disciples seldom have more than a superficial knowledge of divine things.
35:
The crossing ends a long day. Henry observes that after labouring all day in word and doctrine, instead of reposing himself he exposed himself. Robertson lists what the day had held, the blasphemous accusation, the visit of his mother and brothers, the retreat from the crowded house to the sea, the parables by the water and then more within doors. Chrysostom asks why the disciples alone were taken and answers that they were to be spectators of the miracle, but taken by themselves so nobody should see how little faith they had; the other boats show that others crossed separately.

The phrase about taking him even as he was is peculiar to this Gospel, and Ellicott thinks it records the impression made on the evangelist's informant by sheer exhaustion after the day's work. Robertson reads it as meaning they took him along without preparation, and adds that the other boats are a detail given here only, so there was a crowd on the lake as well as the shore. Barnes presses the consequence, that they went without food or clothing in a boat ill-fitted for a storm, which made the danger greater and the miracle more striking.

On the storm the comparisons are linguistic. Robertson notes the vivid present tense where the other Gospels use past forms, that one says the squall came down, showing it fell suddenly from the heights, and that the word used is an old one for cyclonic gusts while the first Gospel chooses a word for an upheaval like an earthquake. Ellicott corrects the tenses, that the waves were beating on the boat and it was filling, both describing continuous action.

The cushion is the detail that holds them. Clarke takes it for a little bed of the kind common in small vessels, having seen several in passage boats not much larger than a bolster; the boat itself he thinks was Christ's own, the one that usually waited on him. Ellicott insists on the article, the cushion commonly found in a boat's stern rather than a pillow brought aboard, and marks the question that follows as this evangelist's alone, a touch of despairing expostulation in which the want of faith afterwards reproved is already traceable. Robertson observes that stern and cushion are both mentioned here, the other Gospels recording only the sleeping. Wesley apologises for the English word, which serves for want of a proper term for that part of the vessel near the rudder.

The command itself draws the strongest language. Barnes finds something exceedingly authoritative and majestic in it, a man standing amid the tempest on a heaving sea in the dark and stilling the waves by his own power, and says none but the God of the storms could awe the elements with a word; Clarke asks the same question outright, who but God could act thus. Ellicott renders the two words as be still and be silenced, noting that the second is used of the guest who had no wedding garment, and observes how vividly the words spoken to the sea are preserved here, as though it were a hostile power in rebellion against its Lord.

Bede reads the scene as a figure: the ship is the tree of the passion, by which the faithful reach the safe shore, and the other ships are those who hold the faith of the cross and are not beaten about by the whirlwind of tribulation. On the rebuke that follows the calm, Clarke answers with the circumstances, that they had him with them and proof enough of his power, while Robertson locates the failure precisely: they had accepted him as Messiah and not yet drawn the conclusions from it, never having come to feel that he was Lord of nature too. At the close Robertson notes that they feared a great fear, where the other accounts say only that they marvelled.
